analogy.p: Think of a castle protecting its treasure. The firewall is the gatehouse guard checking who may enter, anti-malware is the patrol searching for intruders already inside, access levels are the locked doors inside so a guest cannot reach the treasury, passwords are the keys, encryption is the treasure locked in an unbreakable box so a thief who steals it cannot open it, and physical security is the walls and moat. Penetration testing is hiring a friendly burglar to find the weak spots. Where it breaks down: a castle's walls are fixed, but computer defences must be updated constantly as new attacks appear, and attackers can come from anywhere in the world at once.

bullets: A **vulnerability** is a weakness that could be exploited; **prevention** reduces the chance of an attack succeeding, while **identification** (such as penetration testing) finds weaknesses before attackers do.

Think of the seven methods as protecting different things: **people** (passwords, access levels, training), **software** (anti-malware, updates), **the network** (firewall, encryption) and **the building** (physical security).

Every threat from 1.4.1 has matching defences: malware with anti-malware, brute force with strong passwords, interception with encryption, DoS with firewalls and filtering, social engineering with training.
No single method is enough: a firewall will not stop an employee opening a malicious attachment, and encryption does not stop a stolen password being used.
Security always involves a trade-off: stronger security can make a system slower or less convenient for users, and costs money.
Exam questions often give a scenario and ask you to **choose and justify** methods, so always link the method to the specific threat in the scenario.
Higher-level extension: security measures are **preventative** (stop attacks), **detective** (spot them, such as anti-malware scans and logs) and **corrective** (recover, such as backups).
core.h: What the specification asks: identifying and preventing vulnerabilities
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.4.2 asks you to know the common methods used to **identify and prevent vulnerabilities**: **penetration testing**, **anti-malware software**, **firewalls**, **user access levels**, **passwords**, **encryption** and **physical security**. For each you must be able to say what it is, how it works and which threats it protects against. No method is perfect on its own, so organisations use several together, an approach called **defence in depth** or layered security.

bullets: **Purpose**: to identify vulnerabilities, which is different from the other methods that mainly prevent attacks.
It is **authorised and agreed in advance**, with a defined scope, so it is legal and does not accidentally damage live services. Unauthorised hacking is a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
Typical steps: plan and agree scope, carry out the simulated attack, report the weaknesses found, fix them, retest, and repeat regularly.
It can test **software** (for example looking for SQL injection), **networks** (open ports, weak firewall rules), and **people** (sending test phishing emails).
**Benefits**: finds real weaknesses, shows how serious they are, helps meet legal duties to protect data, and builds customer trust.
**Limitations**: it only shows weaknesses at the time of the test, costs money and needs skilled staff, so it must be repeated whenever the system changes.
Pen testing is used by banks, online shops and government bodies, and often follows major software updates.
core.p: **Penetration testing** (pen testing) is when an organisation pays skilled, authorised specialists, often called **ethical or white-hat hackers**, to attack its own systems in a controlled and legal way to find weaknesses. The testers try the same techniques a criminal would, such as exploiting unpatched software, guessing passwords or tricking staff. They then write a report describing what they found, so the organisation can fix the problems before a real attacker finds them.

bullets: **Real-time (on-access) scanning** checks files as they are opened, downloaded or received; **scheduled full scans** check everything on the drive.
**Signature-based detection** compares code with a list of known malware; it cannot detect brand-new malware that is not yet in the list, which is why updates matter.
**Heuristic detection** looks for suspicious behaviour, such as a program trying to encrypt many files or change system settings.
When malware is found the software can **quarantine** it (isolate it so it cannot run), **delete** it or **clean** the infected file, and alert the user.
It protects against viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware and spyware, and can block dangerous websites and email attachments.
**Limitations**: it cannot stop social engineering or a user giving away a password, may slow the computer, and can miss very new malware.
Good practice: keep it switched on, keep it updated, scan removable media before opening, and use it together with a firewall and software updates.
core.p: **Anti-malware software** (including antivirus) is software that **detects, blocks and removes malware**. It scans files, emails, downloads and running programs, and compares them against a database of known malware **signatures**. Because new malware appears every day, the database must be **updated regularly**, otherwise new threats are missed. Most products also use **heuristic** checks, which look for suspicious behaviour so that unknown malware can be caught.

bullets: **How it works**: each packet is examined, and the firewall checks details such as the **source and destination IP address** and the **port number** against its rules, then allows or blocks it.
It can **block traffic from specific addresses**, block certain **ports** or services, and stop unauthorised programs on the computer from sending data out.
It helps protect against **hacking attempts, some malware and some DoS traffic**, because unusual or unwanted traffic can be filtered out.
Firewall rules need to be **configured and kept up to date** by the network manager; a badly configured firewall may block genuine traffic or let attackers in.

**Limitations**: it cannot stop malware that a user downloads and allows, cannot stop social engineering, does not protect against attacks from inside the network, and does not scan the content of encrypted traffic.
In a school or office the firewall sits at the boundary between the **LAN** and the Internet, protecting every device behind it.
A firewall does not remove malware that is already on the computer; that is the job of anti-malware software.
core.p: A **firewall** monitors **incoming and outgoing network traffic** and decides whether to allow or block each packet according to a set of **rules**. It sits between a computer or network and an untrusted network such as the Internet, acting like a security guard at the entrance. A firewall can be **hardware** (a dedicated device or built into a router) or **software** (on a single computer), and it is a key defence against unauthorised access to a network.

bullets: **Typical permissions**: no access, **read only**, **read and write**, and **full control** (which includes deleting and changing permissions).

**Example in a school**: students can read shared resources and save to their own folder; teachers can also see their classes' work; only the network manager (administrator) can install software or change settings.
**Why it helps**: if malware infects a low-level account it cannot change system files or reach sensitive data, so the damage is limited.
It reduces the risk of **insider threats** and accidental deletion, and supports data protection because only authorised staff can see personal data.
Access levels depend on users being **identified**, so they work together with usernames and passwords.
Access must be reviewed: accounts of people who leave should be removed, and permissions changed when roles change.
**Limitation**: if an attacker steals an administrator password they receive all that account's rights, so admin accounts need especially strong protection.
core.p: **User access levels** (also called access rights or permissions) control **which data, programs and areas of a system each user can see, change or delete**. Users are put into groups such as administrator, staff and student, and each group gets only the access it needs for its job. This follows the principle of **least privilege**: give people the minimum access they need. It limits damage if an account is hacked or if a user makes a mistake or acts dishonestly.

bullets: **Strong password rules**: at least 8 characters (longer is much better), a mix of **upper case, lower case, numbers and symbols**, and not based on names, birthdays or common words such as password or 123456.
**Use a different password for every account**, so one breach does not unlock everything; a password manager can store them.
**Never share passwords or write them where others can see them**; this defends against shouldering and blagging.
**Maths of strength**: 8 lower-case letters give 26^8 = 208,827,064,576 combinations, but using 94 typeable characters gives about 6 quadrillion (94^8), making brute force far slower.
**Account lockout** after several failed attempts and **CAPTCHA** tests make online guessing impractical.
**Two-factor authentication** (a password plus a code sent to a phone) and **biometrics** (fingerprint, face) add a second check, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
Passwords should be **stored in encrypted (hashed) form**, not plain text, so a stolen database does not reveal them.
**Limitations**: users choose weak passwords, forget them or are tricked into giving them away through phishing.
core.p: A **password** proves that a user is who they claim to be, so that only authorised people can log in. A **strong password** is hard to guess and hard to crack by brute force. The strength comes mainly from **length** and from using a large pool of characters, and from being **unpredictable** (not a dictionary word or personal detail). Passwords are the most common prevention method and are often the first line of defence for every account.

bullets: **Example (Caesar cipher)**: shift every letter along the alphabet by a key of 3, so HELLO becomes KHOOR; decrypting shifts each letter back by 3. It is easy to break, but it shows the idea of an algorithm and key.
**In transit**: HTTPS websites encrypt data between browser and server, and WPA2 or WPA3 encrypt Wi-Fi traffic, defeating packet sniffers on the network.
**At rest**: stored data on laptops, phones, USB drives and databases can be encrypted, so a stolen device does not reveal its contents.
**Defends against**: data interception, data theft and stolen devices; encrypted passwords stored by websites protect users if the database is stolen.
A longer key and a stronger algorithm make encryption harder to break by brute force.
**Limitations**: it does not stop malware, DoS or social engineering; if the key is stolen or guessed the data is exposed; and encrypting and decrypting needs processing power.
Ransomware misuses encryption: the attacker encrypts the victim's files and keeps the key until payment.
core.p: **Encryption** is the process of converting data from **plaintext** into **ciphertext**, using an algorithm and a **key**, so that it cannot be understood if it is intercepted or stolen. Only someone with the correct key can **decrypt** it back into readable plaintext. Encryption does not stop data being captured, but it makes the captured data useless. It protects data **in transit** across a network and data **stored** on devices.

bullets: **Locks and keycards or PIN door entry** on server rooms so only authorised staff can enter.
**Biometric entry** (fingerprint or face recognition) is harder to copy or share than a key or card.
**CCTV and alarms** deter intruders and provide evidence; **security guards** and visitor sign-in with ID badges control who is on site.
**Locking down devices**: cable locks on laptops, locked cabinets, and disabling or blocking **USB ports** to prevent data theft and malware.
**Protecting from damage**: fireproof or secure safes for backups, fire suppression, and controlled temperature in server rooms.
**Disposal and screens**: shred confidential paper, securely wipe old drives, and use privacy screens or position screens away from windows to stop shouldering.
**Limitation**: physical security protects the building and devices but cannot stop remote attacks across the Internet.
core.p: **Physical security** protects the actual hardware, rooms and buildings where computer systems and data are kept. Software defences are useless if someone can simply walk in and steal a server, plug in a USB drive or read a screen. Physical measures stop **unauthorised physical access** and protect equipment from theft, damage and tampering.

bullets: **Updates and patches** for the operating system, browser and applications close known vulnerabilities; unpatched systems are a common route for worms and ransomware.
**Regular backups** (kept offline or in a separate location) allow data to be restored after ransomware, hardware failure or deletion.
**Staff training** teaches people to spot phishing, never share passwords and challenge strangers; it is the main defence against social engineering.
**Network policy** sets clear, enforced rules on passwords, acceptable use, access, updates and removable media, fixing the 'poor network policy' weakness.
**Monitoring and logs** record logins and unusual activity so attacks can be detected and investigated.
**Validation of input** on websites defends against SQL injection (see programming topics).
These measures are cheap compared with the cost of a breach, so they often give the best value.
core.h: Software updates and other supporting measures
core.p: Although the specification lists seven main methods, mark schemes also credit supporting measures that close vulnerabilities. **Software updates (patches)** fix security weaknesses that the manufacturer has found, so installing them stops attackers using known flaws. Others include backups, staff training and a clear network policy. They make the seven main methods more effective.

bullets: **Malware**: anti-malware scans and removes it; software updates close the hole it uses; access levels limit what it can change.
**Phishing, blagging, shouldering**: staff training, procedures to verify callers, privacy screens, spam filters and two-factor authentication.
**Brute force**: strong, long passwords; account lockout; CAPTCHA; two-factor authentication.
**DoS/DDoS**: firewall and traffic filtering to block unusual requests, plus extra capacity.
**Data interception**: encryption (HTTPS, WPA2), avoiding public Wi-Fi, using a VPN.
**Data theft**: access levels, encryption of stored data, locked rooms and disabled USB ports.
**SQL injection**: validate and sanitise input, use parameterised queries, penetration testing to find the weakness.
**Poor network policy**: write and enforce a clear policy, train staff, and review it regularly.
core.p: A very common exam skill is selecting the **best defence for a named threat**, and explaining why it works. The reasoning always follows the same pattern: say what the defence does, then say how that stops or reduces the specific attack. Good answers avoid just listing methods without linking them to the scenario.

bullets: **Structure for 6 marks**: pick three or four methods; for each say what it is, how it works, and what threat it stops; add a limitation; finish with a conclusion.
**Cost versus benefit**: a small business may choose free anti-malware and strong passwords first; a bank adds penetration testing, encryption and biometric access.
**Convenience versus security**: strict passwords and two-factor authentication slow users down but greatly reduce risk.
**Human factor**: technical tools fail if people choose weak passwords or fall for phishing, so training is essential.
**Ongoing process**: software must be updated, rules reviewed and tests repeated, because new threats appear constantly.

**Link to other topics**: encryption links to data representation and networks; access levels link to databases and user accounts; the Data Protection Act links to legal and ethical issues in Paper 1.
A strong conclusion states the most important measure for the scenario and justifies it.
core.h: Evaluating methods and answering longer questions
core.p: Longer questions ask you to **discuss** or **evaluate** security measures. The top marks go to answers that give several methods, explain how each works, mention a limitation and reach a justified conclusion tailored to the scenario. Do not simply say 'it keeps data safe'; say what exactly it stops and why. A balanced answer shows that layered security is stronger than any single method.

exam: 'State' or 'name' (1 mark): one method only, for example 'firewall'; 'give one way' needs a single clear method.
'Describe' a method (2 to 3 marks): say what it does and how it works, for example a firewall 'monitors traffic and blocks it according to rules'.
'Explain how X protects Y' (3 to 4 marks): method, how it works, and the threat it stops, linked with because or so.
Always link the method to the named threat in the scenario: encryption to interception, anti-malware to viruses, strong passwords to brute force.
Use the exact terms: plaintext, ciphertext, key, signatures, rules, quarantine, access levels, ethical hacker.
Anti-malware answers earn marks for 'scans files', 'compares with a database of known malware' and 'database updated regularly'.
Firewall answers earn marks for 'monitors incoming and outgoing traffic', 'checks against rules' and 'blocks unauthorised traffic'.
Do not write 'stops hackers' alone; say how: blocks, encrypts, restricts, detects, deters.
6-mark discuss questions: three or four methods, each with how it works and a limitation, then a justified conclusion for the scenario.
Mention updates and training as extra credit points, because several mark schemes accept them as prevention.
Calculation tip: combinations = characters^length; show the working to prove longer passwords are stronger.
Encryption questions: always state that the data is scrambled so it is unreadable to anyone without the key.

mistakes.r: A firewall filters network traffic using rules; anti-malware software scans for and removes malware.
mistakes.w: A firewall removes viruses from the computer.

mistakes.r: Encryption does not stop interception; it makes intercepted data unreadable without the key.
mistakes.w: Encryption stops hackers getting the data.

mistakes.r: A strong password is long, unpredictable and mixes upper case, lower case, numbers and symbols.
mistakes.w: A strong password is one that is hard to remember.

mistakes.r: It is authorised, simulated hacking by specialists to find weaknesses so they can be fixed.
mistakes.w: Penetration testing is when criminals hack a company.

mistakes.r: Its database of signatures must be updated regularly so new malware is detected.
mistakes.w: Anti-malware only needs to be installed once.

mistakes.r: Access levels control what each logged-in user can see, edit or delete, limiting damage.
mistakes.w: Access levels stop people logging in.

mistakes.r: Physical security means locks, CCTV, guards and similar measures that protect hardware and buildings.
A firewall cannot stop social engineering, malware the user allows, or attacks from inside; several layers are needed.
mistakes.w: Using a firewall means the network is completely safe.

mistakes.r: It protects confidentiality only; it does not stop malware, DoS or a stolen key.
mistakes.w: Encryption makes data safe from everything.

summary: OCR J277 1.4.2 asks you to know the main ways of identifying and preventing vulnerabilities in computer systems and networks: penetration testing, anti-malware software, firewalls, user access levels, passwords, encryption and physical security. For each you need to say what it is, how it works and which threat it stops. It matters because Paper 1 security questions ask you to match methods to threats and justify your choices.

terms.d: Authorised, simulated attacks on a system by specialists to identify vulnerabilities so they can be fixed.
Software that detects, blocks and removes malware by scanning files and comparing them with known malware signatures.
A recognisable pattern of code that identifies a known piece of malware.
Detecting malware by looking for suspicious behaviour rather than matching a known signature.
Isolating a suspected malicious file so that it cannot run or spread.
Hardware or software that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks or allows it according to a set of rules.
Permissions that control which data and resources each user or group can view, edit or delete.
Giving users only the minimum access they need to do their job.
A long, unpredictable password using a mix of upper case, lower case, numbers and symbols.
Checking identity using two different pieces of evidence, such as a password and a code sent to a phone.
Using a unique physical feature, such as a fingerprint or face, to identify a user.
Converting plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key so it cannot be understood if intercepted.
Data in its original readable form before encryption.
The scrambled, unreadable output produced by encrypting plaintext.
The value used by an encryption algorithm to encrypt and decrypt data.
Measures such as locks, CCTV and guards that protect hardware and buildings from unauthorised physical access.
A fix released by the manufacturer that removes a security weakness or bug.
Using several layers of security so that if one fails others still protect the system.

worked.ans: PIN: 10 seconds. Password: about 208.8 million seconds (about 6.6 years). A longer password with more possible characters is vastly harder to brute-force.
worked.q: A PIN uses 4 digits (0 to 9). A password uses 8 lower-case letters. A program tries 1,000 guesses per second. Compare the maximum time to brute-force each. [4 marks]
steps: Divide by 86,400 seconds per day: about 2,417 days, which is about 6.6 years.

worked.q: A Caesar cipher uses a key of 3 (each letter moves 3 places forward in the alphabet). (a) Encrypt CAT. (b) Decrypt KHOOR. [4 marks]
steps: (a) C moves forward 3 to F, A moves to D, T moves to W.
(b) To decrypt move each letter back 3: K to H, H to E, O to L, O to L, R to O.

worked.ans: Firewall checks traffic against rules and blocks unauthorised access from the Internet; access levels restrict who can view or edit the records, so only authorised staff can change them and damage from a compromised account is limited.
worked.q: A school stores student records on a network connected to the Internet. Explain how a firewall and user access levels help to protect the records. [4 marks]
steps: The firewall monitors traffic entering and leaving the network and checks it against a set of rules.
It blocks unauthorised traffic, for example from unknown addresses or ports, so outsiders cannot reach the records.
User access levels give each user only the permissions they need, such as read only for most staff.
This limits damage and stops students or hacked accounts from viewing or changing the records.
